title: Tennessee Civics (U.S. Government & Civics)
description: Tennessee Civics (U.S. Government & Civics) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A Knoxville neighborhood association discovers its city charter was written so residents elect the council every two years and can remove members at a recall vote. A speaker says this design shows where governing authority truly starts. Which idea is she naming?
questions.correctAnswer: The people themselves hold ultimate authority and lend power to government through elections
distractors: A hereditary council holds authority passed down through founding families
Federal judges hold authority because they serve the longest terms
The city manager holds authority because staff run daily operations
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people are the source of government power. Elections and recall votes are ways citizens grant power to officials and take it back when officials lose public trust.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Authority starts with voters, not with the officeholders they hire.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of residents casting ballots at a neighborhood polling place outside a brick civic building in morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Popular sovereignty: the people are the source of power.
img.title: POWER STARTS WITH PEOPLE

questions.question: A Memphis police lieutenant is filmed parking illegally, is ticketed by one of her own officers, and pays the fine without protest. Commentators call the scene a small civics lesson. Which principle does it illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: The rule of law, meaning legal rules bind officials and private citizens alike
distractors: Civil disobedience, meaning officials may ignore minor laws in public
Executive immunity, meaning supervisors cannot be fined while employed
Home rule, meaning a city may excuse its own employees from fines
questions.explanation: The rule of law means no person stands above the law, including the people who enforce it. When an officer tickets a superior and the superior pays, status does not override the legal rule.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A uniform is not a pass around the law.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a uniformed supervisor handing payment to a clerk at a courthouse window while other residents wait in the same line. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rule of law: nobody is above the law.
img.title: THE LAW BINDS EVERYONE

questions.question: A Chattanooga book club reads a 1689-to-1776 excerpt arguing that individuals enter society already holding rights to life, liberty and property, and that a ruler who attacks those rights breaks a trust. Whose argument is the club reading?
questions.correctAnswer: John Locke, whose natural-rights and consent theory shaped the Declaration of Independence
distractors: Thomas Hobbes, whose theory held that subjects can never resist a sovereign
Baron de Montesquieu, whose theory concerned only the size of legislatures
King George III, whose replies defended taxing the colonies without consent
questions.explanation: John Locke argued that people hold natural rights before government exists and that government rests on consent and trust. Thomas Jefferson drew directly on Locke when drafting the Declaration of Independence.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Locke: rights come first, rulers serve on trust.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of readers around a wooden library table with an old bound volume open beside a window overlooking a river bluff. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Locke taught natural rights and government by consent.
img.title: RIGHTS BEFORE GOVERNMENT

questions.question: At a July picnic in Franklin, a reader recites a long middle section of a 1776 document cataloguing a king's repeated injuries, including taxing without consent and dissolving assemblies. What is that section of the document doing?
questions.correctAnswer: Listing grievances against King George III to justify independence to the world
distractors: Proposing the structure of a new Congress for the united colonies
Granting pardons to soldiers who had served in the royal army
Setting tax rates that the new states would collect each year
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence devotes its long middle section to grievances against King George III. The list was meant to prove to a candid world that separation was necessary, not impulsive.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The grievance list is the evidence file for independence.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of families on picnic blankets at dusk listening to a reader at a small podium beside a flagpole in a town square. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Independence came with a list of reasons.
img.title: THE CASE FOR INDEPENDENCE

questions.question: A Murfreesboro civics class debates a mayor who claims that winning 51 percent once gives her a permanent mandate to ignore later elections. Students answer with a phrase from 1776 about where just powers come from. Which phrase settles the debate?
questions.correctAnswer: The consent of the governed
distractors: The divine right of kings
The supremacy of the executive
The privileges of incumbency
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence states that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Consent is renewed through elections, so no single victory creates permanent authority.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Consent is renewed at elections, never granted forever.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of high school students debating around a seminar table with a model city hall and ballot box on a side counter. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Just powers come from consent of the governed.
img.title: POWER BY PERMISSION ONLY

questions.question: Traders in 1785 watch each state tax goods crossing its border, issue its own paper money, and ignore a treaty the national Congress signed abroad. A merchant asks which governing plan produced this fragmentation. Which plan is it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Articles of Confederation, which kept sovereignty with the states and left Congress unable to tax or enforce decisions
distractors: The Constitution of 1787, which gave Congress direct power to tax individuals
The Northwest Ordinance, which organized territories but governed the states
The Bill of Rights, which limited a strong Congress the states had created
questions.explanation: Under the Articles of Confederation the states kept sovereignty while Congress lacked power to tax, regulate interstate trade, or enforce treaties. Those failures drove the call for the Philadelphia Convention of 1787.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Articles could ask states for money but could not require it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of horse-drawn wagons halted at a state border toll post while merchants examine different paper bills on a table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Articles left the center too weak to act.
img.title: A CONFEDERATION THAT STALLED

questions.question: Debt-burdened farmers in western Massachusetts seize a courthouse in 1786 to stop foreclosure trials, and the Confederation Congress cannot raise funds or troops to respond. Which uprising convinced many leaders that a stronger union was urgent?
questions.correctAnswer: Shays' Rebellion
distractors: The Whiskey Rebellion
The Boston Tea Party
Pontiac's Rebellion
questions.explanation: Shays' Rebellion, led by Daniel Shays, exposed the Confederation government's inability to maintain order or fund a response. It strengthened support for replacing the Articles with the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Shays showed weakness has a price: disorder fills the gap.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of farmers in worn winter clothing gathered outside a stone courthouse while a rider departs down a muddy road. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A government that cannot respond invites crisis.
img.title: FARMERS CLOSE THE COURTHOUSE

questions.question: For a school lobby display in Johnson City, students arrange six cards naming the aims of a famous introduction: form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty. Where do those six aims appear?
questions.correctAnswer: In the Preamble to the United States Constitution
distractors: In the first paragraph of the Bill of Rights
In the closing article of the Articles of Confederation
In the oath that federal judges take at investiture
questions.explanation: The Preamble introduces the Constitution and lists six purposes for the new government. It states goals but grants no power by itself; the articles that follow supply the actual powers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Six goals live in one opening paragraph: the Preamble.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of students placing six plain cards in a row on a display table beneath a framed parchment in a school lobby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Preamble lists six goals for government.
img.title: SIX GOALS, ONE PARAGRAPH

questions.question: A Nashville law professor tells students that a large republic can control mischief by ambition-driven groups better than a small one, because competing groups check each other. Which essay is she teaching?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalist No. 10, Madison's argument that an extended republic controls the effects of factions
distractors: Federalist No. 51, Madison's argument about ambition counteracting ambition among branches
Common Sense, Paine's argument for immediate independence from Britain
Brutus No. 1, an Anti-Federalist warning against a distant national government
questions.explanation: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison argued that factions cannot be eliminated without destroying liberty, so their effects must be controlled. A large republic multiplies interests so no single faction easily dominates.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: More interests competing means no faction rules alone.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a professor gesturing toward a seminar room diagram of many overlapping circles while graduate students take notes. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federalist No. 10: control faction effects, not liberty.
img.title: MANY FACTIONS, SAFER REPUBLIC

questions.question: During ratification debates, skeptics in several states refuse to support the new Constitution until supporters pledge that a list of protected liberties will be added right after the government launches. Which group extracted that pledge, and what did it produce?
questions.correctAnswer: The Anti-Federalists, whose pressure produced the Bill of Rights
distractors: The Federalists, whose own platform already listed the liberties
The Loyalists, whose claims produced a charter of property rights
The abolitionists, whose petitions produced the Reconstruction Amendments
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists attacked the Constitution for lacking a bill of rights and feared an overpowerful national government. Federalist promises of amendments helped win ratification, and Congress proposed the Bill of Rights in 1789.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ratification was secured with a promise paid in rights.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of delegates debating in a modest colonial hall while a clerk carries a parchment page toward an open doorway. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A promised list of rights won ratification.
img.title: THE PROMISE BEHIND RATIFICATION

questions.question: Supporters of a proposed change to the national charter celebrate a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress, but a veteran staffer warns that nothing has been adopted yet. Under Article V, what remains before the change counts?
questions.correctAnswer: Ratification by three-fourths of the state legislatures or state conventions
distractors: A signing ceremony by the President in the Oval Office
A confirming opinion from the Supreme Court
A simple majority in one national popular referendum
questions.explanation: Article V requires two steps: proposal, usually by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, and ratification by three-fourths of the states. The President plays no formal role in the amendment process.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress proposes; the states decide whether it counts.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of legislators applauding in a chamber while a staffer points toward a wall map dotted with state capitol buildings. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Amendments need three-fourths of the states to ratify.
img.title: PROPOSED IS NOT ADOPTED

questions.question: A trucking firm follows a Tennessee equipment rule, then learns a valid federal safety rule for interstate carriers directly contradicts it. Counsel tells the firm which rule a court will enforce. Which clause gives that answer?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supremacy Clause, under which valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law
distractors: The Tenth Amendment, under which state law prevails inside state borders
The Full Faith and Credit Clause, under which each state picks its own rule
The Commerce Clause, under which the most recent rule always prevails
questions.explanation: Article VI's Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, valid federal statutes, and treaties the supreme law of the land. In a genuine conflict, a valid federal rule displaces the conflicting state rule.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Supreme means federal law wins a true conflict.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two freight trucks at a highway inspection station while an inspector compares two rule folders under an overhead gantry. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Supremacy Clause: valid federal law wins conflicts.
img.title: WHEN RULES COLLIDE

questions.question: A poster in a Clarksville classroom has three columns: national duties such as coining money, state duties such as running elections for state offices, and shared duties such as taxing and building roads. Which arrangement does the poster map?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism, the division of power between a national government and state governments
distractors: Unitary government, where one central authority holds all power
Confederation, where a central office only advises sovereign states
Separation of powers, where one government splits work among three branches
questions.explanation: Federalism divides governing authority between national and state governments, each with real powers of its own. Some powers are exclusive to one level, while taxing, borrowing, and courts are concurrent powers both levels share.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federalism means two levels, each with real power.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a two-story civic building at dusk with both floors lit, a flag above the roof and a state seal shape on the lower facade as a plain emblem without lettering. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federalism divides power between two levels.
img.title: TWO LEVELS, REAL POWER

questions.question: A Tennessee county sheriff enforces state theft and assault laws, operates a county jail, and patrols state highways under authority the national Constitution never assigns to Washington. From which source does that state authority flow?
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
distractors: Delegated powers listed for Congress in Article I
Implied powers created by the Necessary and Proper Clause
Treaty powers shared jointly with foreign governments
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the national government, and not prohibited to the states, to the states or to the people. Ordinary criminal law enforcement rests on that reserved state police power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: What was never delegated stayed reserved to the states.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a sheriff's patrol vehicle on a rural highway at dusk with a small county courthouse visible in the valley below. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Reserved powers stay with states or the people.
img.title: THE STATE POLICE POWER

questions.question: A state treasurer proposes printing state paper currency and signing a trade pact with a neighboring country, and lawyers block both ideas the same afternoon. Which category contains the blocked powers?
questions.correctAnswer: Delegated powers granted to the national government by the Constitution
distractors: Reserved powers retained by every state government
Concurrent powers exercised jointly by both levels
Inherent powers belonging to any local government
questions.explanation: Coining money and conducting foreign relations are delegated, or enumerated, powers of the national government. The Constitution also expressly denies states the power to coin money or enter treaties.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Delegated means handed to the national government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of state officials handing a ring of large brass keys up marble steps toward a federal building entrance in morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Delegated powers belong to the national government.
img.title: POWERS HANDED TO WASHINGTON

questions.question: Congress creates a national air traffic safety network even though aircraft appear nowhere in the Constitution, defending the program as a means of regulating travel and trade among the states. Which clause is Congress relying on?
questions.correctAnswer: The Necessary and Proper Clause, which supports implied powers to carry out listed powers
distractors: The Preamble, which grants Congress any power serving the general welfare
The Tenth Amendment, which grants Congress powers the states cannot use
The Supremacy Clause, which grants Congress powers listed in state laws
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose means for executing its enumerated powers, producing implied powers. The Supreme Court endorsed this reading in McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The ends are listed; the means may stretch to reach them.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an air traffic control tower at dawn guiding passenger jets above runways and hangars spread across a plain. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Implied powers flow from Necessary and Proper.
img.title: OLD CLAUSE, NEW MACHINES

questions.question: Three student teams remodel a classroom government: one drafts rules, one runs the classroom store under those rules, and one judges disputes about the rules' meaning, with no team allowed to do another team's job. Which structural principle are they modeling?
questions.correctAnswer: Separation of powers
distractors: Federalism
Judicial review
Popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides the work of government among legislative, executive, and judicial branches so no single body controls making, enforcing, and judging the law. Montesquieu's writings strongly influenced this design.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three jobs, three separate sets of hands.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three separate worktables in one hall, one with scrolls, one with a seal stamp, and one with a gavel beside balanced scales. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Separation of powers splits government's three jobs.
img.title: THREE JOBS, THREE TABLES

questions.question: Within one month, a president vetoes a spending bill, Congress overrides that veto, and a federal court voids a different statute for violating the First Amendment. A textbook labels the whole sequence with one phrase. Which phrase fits?
questions.correctAnswer: Checks and balances, because each branch used a tool to limit another branch
distractors: Direct democracy, because voters personally settled each dispute
Judicial supremacy, because the court's action ended all debate
Unanimous consent, because every branch agreed before acting
questions.explanation: Checks and balances equip each branch to restrain the others: the presidential veto, the congressional override, and judicial review. The friction is a deliberate safeguard against concentrated power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Vetoes and overrides are the design working, not failing.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three large interlocking stone gears turning against one another above a capitol plaza, each slowing the next. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Checks and balances let branches limit each other.
img.title: FRICTION BY DESIGN

questions.question: In 1803 a cabinet secretary sues for his commission, and the Supreme Court refuses to apply a statute it finds inconsistent with the Constitution itself. Which lasting power did Marbury v. Madison establish?
questions.correctAnswer: Judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional
distractors: Judicial appointment, the power of courts to choose their own judges
Judicial legislation, the power of courts to rewrite flawed statutes
Judicial immunity, the power of courts to pardon convicted officials
questions.explanation: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review. Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that it is the duty of the judicial branch to say what the law is, and that the Constitution outranks any conflicting statute.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury gave courts an eraser for unconstitutional laws.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of robed judges at a high wooden bench in an early American courtroom while a clerk holds two documents side by side. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Judicial review lets courts void unconstitutional laws.
img.title: THE COURT CLAIMS REVIEW

questions.question: Police in Knoxville stop a street preacher for disturbing the peace after officers first shred his handbills, close his reserved park meeting, and refuse his written appeal to the city board. His lawyer groups all four actions under a single amendment. Which one?
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment, which protects speech, press, assembly, and petition together
distractors: The Second Amendment, which protects the keeping and bearing of arms
The Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches
The Sixth Amendment, which protects rights of criminal defendants
questions.explanation: The First Amendment bundles five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition for redress of grievances. Handbills, a public meeting, and a written appeal all fall inside that single amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms share one amendment: count them on one hand.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a speaker at a park pavilion while residents hold blank placards and a clerk accepts a sealed envelope at a nearby table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: First Amendment: speech, press, assembly, petition, religion.
img.title: FIVE FREEDOMS, ONE AMENDMENT

questions.question: A Chattanooga parade applicant who criticizes the mayor is charged a security fee ten times higher than supportive groups pay for the same route, solely because officials dislike his message. Which doctrine makes the fee scheme constitutionally suspect?
questions.correctAnswer: Viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment, because government may not burden speech based on its message
distractors: Prior restraint doctrine, because the parade was banned before it occurred
The establishment doctrine, because the fee funded a religious display
The exclusionary rule, because evidence was gathered without a warrant
questions.explanation: Government may impose reasonable, content-neutral rules for parades, but charging more because officials dislike a speaker's viewpoint is viewpoint discrimination. The First Amendment forbids government from favoring or burdening speech based on its message.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same route, same rules: the message cannot set the price.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two parade groups marching the same street while a clerk at a fee window gestures toward identical empty price boards. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Viewpoint discrimination burdens speech for its message.
img.title: SAME ROUTE, SAME RULES

questions.question: Detectives in Nashville, lacking any court order, force a landlord to unlock a tenant's apartment so they can photograph documents for a fraud case. Which protection is at the center of the tenant's lawsuit?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, normally requiring a warrant based on probable cause
distractors: The First Amendment protection for publishing the photographed documents
The Fifth Amendment protection against being tried twice for one offense
The Seventh Amendment right to a jury in federal civil disputes
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures and generally requires a warrant supported by probable cause. A warrantless, nonconsensual entry into a home is the classic violation the amendment targets.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Homes get the Fourth Amendment's strongest shield.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of officers standing outside a closed apartment door while a judge reviews papers at a desk in an inset courthouse scene. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Fourth Amendment: warrants and probable cause for searches.
img.title: A WARRANT COMES FIRST

questions.question: A Franklin suspect, held for hours without being told she may stay silent or have a lawyer present, confesses, and her attorney moves to exclude the confession. Which pair of protections drives the motion?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and the Miranda warnings that safeguard it during custodial interrogation
distractors: The Third Amendment ban on quartering soldiers and the right to refuse housing
The Ninth Amendment reservation of unlisted rights and the right to travel
The Tenth Amendment reservation of state powers and the right to a local jury
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment provides that no person shall be compelled to testify against himself. In Miranda v. Arizona the Supreme Court required warnings about silence and counsel before custodial interrogation so that right is meaningful.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Silence is a right, and Miranda makes sure you hear it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a detective pausing at an interrogation room door while a defense attorney arrives in the corridor carrying a folder. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Miranda warnings protect the right to stay silent.
img.title: WARNED BEFORE QUESTIONING

questions.question: An indigent defendant in Memphis in 1963 is denied a lawyer, is convicted of a felony, and appeals on the ground that a fair trial was impossible without counsel. Which decision vindicated defendants in his position?
questions.correctAnswer: Gideon v. Wainwright, which required states to provide counsel to defendants who cannot afford one in criminal cases
distractors: Brown v. Board of Education, which required states to desegregate public schools
Mapp v. Ohio, which required states to exclude illegally seized evidence
Baker v. Carr, which required states to hear apportionment challenges in court
questions.explanation: In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. States must appoint counsel for indigent criminal defendants.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gideon: no fair trial without a lawyer you can actually have.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a courtroom where a public defender takes a seat beside a defendant at the defense table before a watching judge. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Gideon guarantees counsel for those who cannot pay.
img.title: A LAWYER FOR THE POOR

questions.question: A judge in Jackson sets bail at a sum wildly beyond a minor defendant's means for a nonviolent charge and adds a fine designed to bankrupt his family, prompting an appeal. Which amendment supplies both challenges?
questions.correctAnswer: The Eighth Amendment, which bars excessive bail and excessive fines and bans cruel and unusual punishments
distractors: The Second Amendment, which bars excessive restrictions on firearms
The Fourth Amendment, which bars excessive force during arrests only
The Ninth Amendment, which bars excessive federal regulation generally
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment prohibits excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments. Bail must be tied to ensuring appearance and safety, not set as punishment before trial.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eighth Amendment: bail and fines must stay proportionate.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of balanced scales on a judge's bench beside a modest stack of coins while a young defendant and parent look on. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and fines.
img.title: BAIL MUST FIT THE CASE

questions.question: A state law in 1952 assigns Black children in Topeka to separate schools, and lawyers argue the assignment itself stamps children with inferiority even where buildings match. Which ruling ended the legal doctrine behind that assignment?
questions.correctAnswer: Brown v. Board of Education, which held that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal
distractors: Plessy v. Ferguson, which held that separate facilities could satisfy equality
Dred Scott v. Sandford, which held that citizenship excluded enslaved people
Regents v. Bakke, which held that racial quotas in admissions were unlawful
questions.explanation: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court unanimously held that separating children in public schools solely by race violates the Equal Protection Clause. The decision rejected the separate-but-equal doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson in public education.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Brown: separate schools are inherently unequal.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of children of different backgrounds walking together up the steps of a brick schoolhouse in bright morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Brown ended separate-but-equal in public schools.
img.title: ONE SCHOOLHOUSE DOOR

questions.question: After the Civil War, a Southern state writes a rule that only men whose grandfathers voted may register, aiming to restore voting rolls from before emancipation. Which amendment's ban on racial voting discrimination does the rule collide with?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifteenth Amendment, which forbids denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
distractors: The Twelfth Amendment, which forbids faithless voting by presidential electors
The Seventeenth Amendment, which forbids literacy tests for Senate voters
The Twenty-first Amendment, which forbids poll taxes in federal elections
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibits the United States or any state from denying the right to vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. Grandfather clauses were devices built to evade that ban.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteenth: race can never be a voting qualification.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens of different generations lining up at a registration table outside a county courthouse in autumn light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Fifteenth Amendment bans racial voting discrimination.
img.title: RACE OFF THE BALLOT RULES

questions.question: Women in Nashville in August 1920 wait by telegraph wires as one final state decides whether a constitutional change will take effect nationwide. Which change did Tennessee's ratification complete that month?
questions.correctAnswer: The Nineteenth Amendment, guaranteeing that the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex
distractors: The Eighteenth Amendment, guaranteeing women equal pay in federal employment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment, guaranteeing voting rights in school board elections
The Equal Rights Amendment, guaranteeing equality under state family laws
questions.explanation: Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the Nineteenth Amendment in August 1920, supplying the final ratification needed. The amendment bars denying the right to vote on account of sex.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tennessee was the Perfect 36 for women's suffrage.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of women in 1920 dress gathered around a telegraph office window at dusk while a clerk raises a message slip overhead. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Nineteenth Amendment: sex cannot bar voting.
img.title: THE PERFECT THIRTY-SIX

questions.question: A 19-year-old soldier shipping out in 1971 asks why he can be drafted to fight abroad yet, under older state rules, could not vote for the leaders sending him. Which amendment answered that complaint nationally?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, which set 18 as the minimum voting age in federal and state elections
distractors: The Twenty-third Amendment, which set 18 as the voting age in presidential elections
The Twenty-fourth Amendment, which set 18 as the age for jury service nationwide
The Twenty-fifth Amendment, which set 18 as the age for holding federal office
questions.explanation: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified in 1971 during the Vietnam War, bars denying the vote to citizens 18 or older on account of age. The slogan of the era was old enough to fight, old enough to vote.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-sixth: 18 is old enough to vote.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a young soldier in uniform placing a ballot into a box while an older veteran poll worker holds the slot open. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Twenty-sixth Amendment set the voting age at 18.
img.title: OLD ENOUGH TO VOTE

questions.question: A Georgia voter in 1963 is turned away from a federal primary for refusing to pay a one-dollar tax receipt demanded at registration. Which amendment later removed that barrier from federal elections?
questions.correctAnswer: The Twenty-fourth Amendment, which banned poll taxes in elections for federal office
distractors: The Fifteenth Amendment, which banned all fees connected with registration
The Nineteenth Amendment, which banned taxes on first-time voters
The Twenty-second Amendment, which banned charges at polling places
questions.explanation: The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964, prohibits poll taxes in primaries and elections for federal office. The Supreme Court later extended the ban to state elections in Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-fourth: no pay-to-vote tax for federal office.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a voter handing an empty wallet gesture to a registrar while other citizens register freely at a counter behind him. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Twenty-fourth Amendment banned federal poll taxes.
img.title: NO PRICE ON THE VOTE

questions.question: Students in Des Moines in 1969 wear black armbands mourning war dead, cause no disruption, and are suspended anyway. Which holding protects expression like theirs in public schools?
questions.correctAnswer: Tinker v. Des Moines: students keep speech rights at school unless expression substantially disrupts school work
distractors: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier: schools may censor any student expression for any reason
Bethel v. Fraser: schools may punish any political symbol as lewd speech
Morse v. Frederick: schools may ban all student speech about public issues
questions.explanation: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court held that students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. Schools may restrict speech only when it would substantially disrupt school operations.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tinker: quiet protest is protected speech at school.

img.tip: Tinker protects nondisruptive student speech.
img.title: ARMBANDS IN THE HALLWAY

questions.question: A delegate-counting exercise gives one chamber 435 members apportioned after each census and the other chamber exactly two members per state regardless of size. Which pair of chambers is the exercise describing?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, apportioned by population, and the Senate, with equal representation per state
distractors: The House of Commons, apportioned by counties, and the House of Lords, with hereditary seats
The Electoral College, apportioned by districts, and the Cabinet, with appointed seats
The General Assembly, apportioned by counties, and the Council of State, with equal seats
questions.explanation: The Constitution apportions the 435-member House among the states by population after each decennial census. The Senate gives every state two senators, so Wyoming and California hold equal Senate weight.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House follows people; Senate treats states as equals.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two chambers side by side, one vast curved hall with many desks and one smaller hall with paired desks, viewed from a gallery. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House by population; Senate equal per state.
img.title: TWO CHAMBERS, TWO LOGICS

questions.question: When the Census Bureau publishes its new state population tables, one state's delegation in Washington grows from nine seats to ten while another state's shrinks from seven to six, even though Congress never voted to change the size of the House. What just happened?
questions.correctAnswer: Reapportionment, the reallocation of House seats among states based on the decennial census
distractors: Redistricting, the redrawing of one state's internal district lines
Gerrymandering, the manipulation of lines for partisan advantage
Apportionment review, the judicial recount of disputed ballots
questions.explanation: Reapportionment reallocates the fixed 435 House seats among the states after each census according to population change. States then redraw their own district maps through redistricting.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reapportionment moves seats between states after the census.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of clerks moving two wooden chairs from one side of a large map table to the other while census ledgers lie open nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Census results shift House seats among states.
img.title: SEATS FOLLOW THE CENSUS

questions.question: Small-state delegates in 1787 threaten to walk out unless every state keeps an equal voice somewhere in the new legislature. Which bargain answered them inside Congress itself?
questions.correctAnswer: The Connecticut Compromise, pairing a population-based House with an equal-vote Senate
distractors: The Three-Fifths Compromise, pairing taxation rules with import duties
The Missouri Compromise, pairing free and slave state admissions
The Great Compromise of 1850, pairing territories with fugitive slave rules
questions.explanation: The Connecticut Compromise merged the Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan. It created a House based on population and a Senate where each state holds two votes, settling the representation deadlock at the Convention.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Population in one house, equality in the other.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of delegates shaking hands across a long table in a colonial assembly room with two chamber sketches pinned behind them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Connecticut Compromise built the two-track Congress.
img.title: THE DEAL THAT SAVED CONGRESS

questions.question: A health-care proposal spends eleven months moving through subcommittee hearings, expert testimony, a markup session, and floor debate before either chamber votes on final passage. Which stage explains most of that delay by design?
questions.correctAnswer: Committee consideration, where most bills are studied, amended, or allowed to die
distractors: Conference reconciliation, where the President merges the two chambers' texts
Judicial preview, where courts approve bills before a vote may occur
State ratification, where legislatures endorse federal bills in advance
questions.explanation: Most congressional work happens in committees and subcommittees, which hold hearings, gather expertise, and mark up bill text. The vast majority of introduced bills never leave committee at all.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Committees are where bills are built or buried.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of legislators and staff around a long committee table stacked with briefing folders while witnesses wait in rows of chairs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Committees study, amend, or bury most bills.
img.title: WHERE BILLS ARE BUILT

questions.question: A president returns a tax bill unsigned with a written message of objections on day nine, and both chambers schedule new votes within the week. If Congress instead had adjourned for the year on day eight, which different outcome was possible?
questions.correctAnswer: A pocket veto, where the unsigned bill dies because adjournment prevents its return
distractors: A line-item approval, where the President enacts only the revenue sections
An automatic override, where silence converts the bill into law at once
A judicial veto, where the Supreme Court decides the bill's fate instead
questions.explanation: A president normally signs a bill, vetoes it with a return message, or lets it become law without a signature after ten days. If Congress adjourns so the bill cannot be returned, presidential inaction kills it: a pocket veto, which Congress cannot override.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No session, no return: a pocket veto cannot be overridden.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an empty congressional chamber with lights dimmed while an unsigned document rests on a desk in a quiet executive office. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A pocket veto kills a bill when Congress adjourns.
img.title: SILENCE THAT KILLS A BILL

questions.question: Forty-one senators keep debate open for a third week to block a voting bill they cannot defeat on a straight vote, and supporters hunt for sixty votes to end the standoff. Which procedure are the supporters seeking?
questions.correctAnswer: Cloture, the Senate vote that limits debate and ends a filibuster
distractors: Reconciliation, the House vote that merges two versions of one bill
Impeachment, the Senate vote that removes an obstructing member
Discharge, the Senate vote that recalls a bill from the President
questions.explanation: Senate Rule XXII allows cloture, which for most legislation requires 60 votes to end extended debate known as a filibuster. Without cloture, a determined minority can delay or block final passage.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sixty votes break a filibuster: that number is cloture.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a senator speaking at a lone podium late at night in a nearly empty chamber while colleagues confer near the doors. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Cloture ends a filibuster, usually needing 60 votes.
img.title: DEBATE WITHOUT END

questions.question: Two leaders trend in the news on the same day: one schedules every bill reaching the House floor, and one presides over the Senate while also standing first in line to act as president if needed. Which offices are in the story?
questions.correctAnswer: The Speaker of the House and the Vice President as President of the Senate
distractors: The House Majority Whip and the Chief Justice of the United States
The Senate Majority Leader and the Secretary of the Senate
The Speaker of the House and the President pro tempore acting alone
questions.explanation: The Speaker is the House's presiding officer and most powerful member, controlling the floor schedule. The Vice President serves as President of the Senate under the Constitution and votes there only to break ties.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Speaker runs the House; the Vice President presides in the Senate.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two podiums in separate chambers, one beneath a large gavel resting on a desk and one beside a single tie-breaking ballot card. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Speaker leads the House; VP presides over the Senate.
img.title: TWO PODIUMS, TWO ROLES

questions.question: Congress regulates a purely local bakery's wheat purchases after finding that thousands of similar purchases together move national grain prices. Opponents call the law a federal overreach. Which power is Congress claiming for the statute?
questions.correctAnswer: The Commerce Clause power to regulate economic activity that substantially affects interstate commerce in the aggregate
distractors: The treaty power to set food standards negotiated with grain exporters
The coinage power to standardize ingredients used in minted products
The naturalization power to set uniform rules for immigrant bakers
questions.explanation: Congress may regulate interstate commerce, and cases such as Wickard v. Filburn hold that local activity can be reached when, in the aggregate, it substantially affects interstate commerce. Courts still require a genuine connection to that enumerated power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Alone it is local; together it moves a national market.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a small bakery storefront connected by glowing road lines to grain elevators and rail yards across a wide landscape. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Commerce power reaches activity affecting national markets.
img.title: ONE BAKERY, NATIONAL MARKET

questions.question: A new federal income tax measure is introduced first in the Senate by a popular senator, and the House refuses to consider it until the paperwork is corrected. Which constitutional rule is the House enforcing?
questions.correctAnswer: Revenue bills must originate in the House of Representatives
distractors: Revenue bills must originate in the Senate Finance Committee
Revenue bills must originate with the Secretary of the Treasury
Revenue bills must originate in states that pay the most tax
questions.explanation: Article I provides that all bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives, though the Senate may propose amendments. The rule ties taxation most directly to the chamber closest to the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tax bills start in the People's House.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a clerk redirecting a folder across a capitol corridor from a small chamber door toward a larger chamber door. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Revenue bills must start in the House.
img.title: TAX BILLS START DOWNSTAIRS

questions.question: A House panel votes articles accusing a federal judge of bribery, and the case moves across the Capitol for a trial where conviction needs a two-thirds vote. Which process is unfolding, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment by the House followed by a trial and possible removal in the Senate
distractors: Indictment by the Senate followed by sentencing in the House
Censure by the House followed by removal through the Supreme Court
Recall by the voters followed by confirmation in the Senate
questions.explanation: Impeachment is a two-step process: the House impeaches by majority vote, functioning like an indictment, and the Senate tries the case. Conviction and removal require two-thirds of the Senate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House accuses; Senate decides removal.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of representatives carrying a sealed folder across a marble rotunda toward a chamber arranged like a courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Impeachment: House charges, Senate tries.
img.title: ACCUSATION CROSSES THE CAPITOL

questions.question: A candidate announcement lists her credentials: natural-born citizen, age 41, and fourteen years a United States resident. Which office's constitutional qualifications has she just recited, word for word in substance?
questions.correctAnswer: President of the United States
distractors: United States Senator
United States Representative
Chief Justice of the United States
questions.explanation: Article II requires the President to be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for 14 years. Senators and representatives face lower age thresholds and a citizenship-duration rule instead.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirty-five, natural-born, fourteen years: that is Article II.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a candidate speaking at an outdoor rally podium with flags behind her and families gathered on a courthouse lawn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Presidential qualifications come from Article II.
img.title: THE ARTICLE TWO CHECKLIST

questions.question: On election night a network projects 538 total electors, and anchors repeat that one number alone decides the presidency. Which number are they repeating, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: 270, the majority of the 538 electoral votes needed to win the presidency
distractors: 435, the size of the House delegation that certifies the result
100, the number of senators who confirm the winning candidate
538, the unanimous total a candidate must reach to take office
questions.explanation: The Electoral College holds 538 electors: 435 House seats plus 100 Senate seats plus 3 for the District of Columbia. A candidate must win an absolute majority, 270 electoral votes, to become President.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Half of 538 plus one: 270 wins the White House.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a television studio election map glowing behind anchors at a desk while tally boards fill with colored state shapes without lettering. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 270 of 538 electoral votes wins the presidency.
img.title: THE MAGIC NUMBER 270

questions.question: A president orders a carrier group toward a crisis while insisting only Congress may formally commit the nation to war. Both claims can be true because the Constitution splits war authority. How is it split?
questions.correctAnswer: The President commands the armed forces as Commander in Chief, while Congress holds the power to declare war
distractors: The President declares war, while Congress commands forces in the field
The Supreme Court declares war, while the President funds the campaign
State governors declare war, while Congress commands the National Guard
questions.explanation: Article II makes the President Commander in Chief of the armed forces. Article I gives Congress, not the President, the power to declare war and to raise and fund armies.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One commands the forces; the other declares the war.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a naval carrier group at sea at dawn viewed from a distant shoreline with a capitol dome silhouette far inland. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: President commands; Congress declares war.
img.title: SPLIT WAR AUTHORITY

questions.question: An ambassador signs an agreement abroad, returns home, and warns the President that the document binds the nation only after a two-thirds Senate vote. What kind of agreement needs that vote?
questions.correctAnswer: A treaty, which requires the advice and consent of two-thirds of the senators present
distractors: An executive order, which requires the consent of the House leadership
A pocket agreement, which requires consent of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
A signing statement, which requires consent of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The President negotiates and signs treaties, but Article II requires the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate for ratification. Lesser international arrangements made as executive agreements follow a different, less formal path.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Treaties need two-thirds of the Senate to bind.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of diplomats exchanging folders across a long table in a formal hall while observers sit in a gallery above. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaties require two-thirds Senate consent.
img.title: TWO-THIRDS TO BIND

questions.question: On his final morning in office, a president frees a former official convicted of a federal fraud offense, erasing the punishment entirely, and Congress can do nothing to reverse it. Which power did he use?
questions.correctAnswer: The presidential pardon power for offenses against the United States
distractors: The presidential amnesty power for offenses against state governments
The presidential reprieve power for overturning jury verdicts at trial
The presidential clemency power for reversing impeachment convictions
questions.explanation: Article II grants the President power to pardon offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment. A full pardon removes the punishment and is not subject to congressional reversal.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pardons cover federal offenses, never impeachment.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a hand signing a document at a large desk in a quiet office as morning light falls across an empty chair opposite. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The pardon power erases federal punishment.
img.title: ONE SIGNATURE, FULL PARDON

questions.question: Fifteen department heads, from Agriculture to Veterans Affairs, brief a new president on budgets running into the trillions and workforces in the millions. Which institution do those fifteen departments form the core of?
questions.correctAnswer: The Cabinet and the federal bureaucracy that carries out the laws day to day
distractors: The federal judiciary that reviews the laws for constitutionality
The congressional leadership that writes the laws each session
The state governments that resist the laws they dislike
questions.explanation: The President leads the executive branch through the Cabinet departments and the wider federal bureaucracy. Those agencies administer programs, write implementing regulations, and deliver services under laws Congress enacts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Laws on paper become services through the bureaucracy.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of officials seated around a long oval table with folders and water glasses while staff stand along the walls of a formal room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Cabinet departments run the laws day to day.
img.title: FIFTEEN DEPARTMENTS AT WORK

questions.question: A president directs an agency to enforce a policy that Congress considered and expressly rejected the year before, and a court strikes the directive down. Which limit on executive orders does the ruling reflect?
questions.correctAnswer: An executive order cannot contradict or override a statute enacted by Congress
distractors: An executive order cannot remain in force longer than ninety days
An executive order cannot be issued during an election year
An executive order cannot address any subject Congress has debated
questions.explanation: Executive orders carry legal force only when grounded in the Constitution or a statute Congress passed. An order that conflicts with a clear congressional enactment exceeds presidential authority, as Youngstown Sheet and Tube v. Sawyer illustrates.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Orders implement the law; they cannot outrank it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge's gavel resting beside a rolled directive scroll on a courthouse bench while an agency building stands outside the window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Executive orders cannot override statutes.
img.title: ORDERS STOP AT STATUTES

questions.question: A vice president spends Monday breaking a 50-50 Senate tie, Tuesday meeting foreign leaders at the White House, and Wednesday preparing to assume the presidency if tragedy strikes. Which document assigns the first of those duties expressly?
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution, which makes the Vice President President of the Senate with a tie-breaking vote
distractors: The Presidential Succession Act, which assigns Senate duties to the Vice President
The Twenty-second Amendment, which assigns legislative duties to the Vice President
The Senate standing rules, which create the office of Vice President
questions.explanation: Article I makes the Vice President the President of the Senate, empowered to vote only when the Senate is equally divided. The office's other modern roles grew through practice and later amendments and statutes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One constitutional Senate job: break the tie.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a presiding officer casting a single ballot in a chamber split evenly down the middle aisle at a moment of stillness. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Vice President breaks Senate ties.
img.title: THE TIE-BREAKING VOTE

questions.question: A contract suit between a Texas seller and a New York buyer over a large sum is filed in federal court even though no federal statute is involved. Which basis for federal jurisdiction makes that filing possible?
questions.correctAnswer: Diversity of citizenship, where parties from different states dispute more than the statutory minimum amount
distractors: Federal question jurisdiction, where a treaty names both parties directly
Original jurisdiction, where the Supreme Court must hear all contract suits
Appellate jurisdiction, where federal courts retry all state contract verdicts
questions.explanation: Federal courts may hear diversity cases: suits between citizens of different states where the amount in controversy exceeds the threshold Congress set, currently 75,000 dollars. Cases raising a federal law or constitutional question instead rest on federal question jurisdiction.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Different states plus a large claim can open federal court.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two business owners from distant skylines meeting with lawyers at a federal courthouse entrance beneath tall columns. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Diversity jurisdiction covers cross-state disputes.
img.title: STRANGERS IN FEDERAL COURT

questions.question: A nominee for the highest court answers Senate questions for four days, wins confirmation by a narrow vote, and will likely serve for decades regardless of later elections. Which design choices create that long, insulated tenure?
questions.correctAnswer: Presidential nomination with Senate confirmation, followed by service during good behavior, effectively for life
distractors: Election by state legislatures, followed by renewable six-year terms
Appointment by the House, followed by removal at each census
Selection by sitting justices, followed by mandatory retirement at seventy
questions.explanation: Article II provides for presidential nomination and Senate confirmation of Supreme Court justices. Article III then protects federal judges with tenure during good behavior and salary protection, insulating them from political retaliation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure is a shield for judicial independence.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a nominee seated alone at a witness table facing a curved panel of senators in a hearing room with photographers along the back wall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Justices are nominated, confirmed, then insulated for life.
img.title: CONFIRMED, THEN INSULATED

questions.question: A young appellate judge privately doubts an old precedent but follows it anyway, writing that lower courts must honor rulings from above even when they suspect change is coming. Which practice is she honoring?
questions.correctAnswer: Stare decisis, the practice of standing by decided precedent
distractors: Judicial activism, the practice of replacing precedent with policy views
Original jurisdiction, the practice of hearing a case first at the top
Amicus practice, the practice of inviting outside briefs in every case
questions.explanation: Stare decisis means courts adhere to precedent so law remains stable and predictable. The Supreme Court may overrule its own precedents, but lower courts must follow controlling rulings until the higher court itself changes them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Precedent binds downward even when doubted.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge in a quiet chambers library reaching for an old bound volume on a shelf of matching volumes stretching into shadow. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Stare decisis keeps courts standing by precedent.
img.title: STANDING BY WHAT WAS DECIDED

questions.question: A ruling comes down 6-3: one opinion speaks for the court, one agrees with the result for different reasons, and one rejects the outcome entirely. Which trio names those three documents, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Majority opinion, concurring opinion, and dissenting opinion
distractors: Plurality opinion, per curiam opinion, and advisory opinion
Majority opinion, veto message, and conference report
Lead opinion, signing statement, and minority report
questions.explanation: The majority opinion states the court's holding and reasoning and controls as precedent. A concurrence agrees with the judgment on different grounds, while a dissent explains why the minority would have decided the case the other way.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Majority rules, concurrence agrees differently, dissent objects.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three stacks of bound opinions on a clerk's desk, the tallest stack centered under a lamp in a marble hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Majority, concurrence, dissent: three voices per ruling.
img.title: THREE VOICES, ONE RULING

questions.question: Two organizations publish platforms, recruit candidates, run registration drives, and try to connect ordinary voters to the officials who govern them. Which function best defines both organizations in a democracy?
questions.correctAnswer: Political parties link citizens to government by organizing elections around competing programs
distractors: Political parties replace government by governing neighborhoods directly
Political parties enforce election law by prosecuting illegal campaigns
Political parties set interest rates by coordinating with central banks
questions.explanation: Political parties serve as linkage institutions: they recruit and nominate candidates, simplify choices through platforms and labels, mobilize voters, and organize the winning side to govern. Interest groups and media perform different linkage roles.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties are the bridge between voters and government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of volunteers at folding tables registering voters outside a community center while candidates greet families near the entrance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Parties link citizens to government through elections.
img.title: THE VOTER-TO-GOVERNMENT BRIDGE

questions.question: In January, party members in one state gather in school gyms to debate and choose delegates face to face, while voters in the neighboring state simply cast secret ballots at polling places. Which pair of nominating methods is on display?
questions.correctAnswer: A caucus, based on open meetings and discussion, versus a primary election, based on voting
distractors: A convention, based on delegate bargaining, versus a referendum, based on direct lawmaking
A runoff, based on a second ballot, versus a recall, based on removal petitions
A straw poll, based on informal surveys, versus a general election, based on voting
questions.explanation: Caucuses are party meetings where members discuss candidates and select delegates or express preferences publicly. Primaries are elections administered like general elections, where voters cast ballots to nominate candidates.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Caucus means gather and argue; primary means vote.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of neighbors debating in a school gymnasium on one side and voters at curtained booths in a polling hall on the other, split down the middle. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Caucuses deliberate; primaries are elections.
img.title: MEET AND DEBATE OR VOTE

questions.question: A nurses association testifies at hearings, drafts model bills, and funds an affiliated committee that contributes to friendly candidates, yet it runs no candidate of its own. Which type of organization is it?
questions.correctAnswer: An interest group seeking to influence policy without taking responsibility for governing
distractors: A political party seeking to win office and control government directly
A government agency seeking to enforce the laws it helped to draft
A media outlet seeking to inform voters about health legislation
questions.explanation: Interest groups try to shape policy from outside government by lobbying, research, litigation, and campaign support through political action committees. Unlike parties, they do not nominate candidates under their own label or govern when they win.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Groups influence policy; parties seek to govern.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of association members presenting charts to legislators in a hearing room while a candidate rally fills a hall visible through glass doors behind them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Interest groups influence without governing.
img.title: INFLUENCE WITHOUT OFFICE

questions.question: For three straight weeks, cable panels and front pages hammer on bridge safety after a collapse, and legislatures that had ignored inspection bills suddenly schedule hearings. Which media power produced that shift?
questions.correctAnswer: Agenda setting, the media's ability to focus public and official attention on selected issues
distractors: Priming, the media's ability to change the standards voters use to judge leaders
Framing, the media's ability to tilt interpretation of one specific event
Gatekeeping, the media's ability to suppress all coverage of rival stories
questions.explanation: Agenda setting describes how heavy coverage signals which issues matter most, pushing them onto the public and policy agendas. Framing and priming concern how issues are interpreted and judged, a step beyond sheer attention.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coverage chooses what the country talks about.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of news cameras aimed at a damaged bridge while legislators in a distant hearing room turn toward wall screens showing the same scene. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Agenda setting moves issues to the center of attention.
img.title: COVERAGE SETS THE AGENDA

questions.question: A pollster interviews 400 randomly chosen voters statewide, reports a close race, and adds that results could be off by about five points either way. Which concept is she warning readers about?
questions.correctAnswer: The margin of sampling error that comes from surveying a sample instead of the whole population
distractors: The bandwagon effect that makes trailing candidates gain support
The margin of victory that officials certify after counting ballots
The sampling frame that lists every registered voter in the state
questions.explanation: Polls survey a random sample to estimate opinion in a larger population, and sampling produces a margin of error that shrinks as sample size grows. A lead smaller than that margin means the race is effectively too close to call from the poll alone.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A sample estimates; the margin admits the uncertainty.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a researcher with a clipboard interviewing a shopper in a market aisle while charts glow on a tablet in her other hand. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Margins of error measure sampling uncertainty.
img.title: HONEST UNCERTAINTY IN POLLS

questions.question: A baby born in a Knoxville hospital to parents who immigrated last year is issued a birth certificate, and a nurse remarks that the document already settles the child's national status. Which rule is she invoking?
questions.correctAnswer: Birthright citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment for persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction
distractors: Naturalization at birth under a statute granting status to hospital births
Derivative citizenship under a treaty covering children of new residents
Jus sanguinis under the Constitution, granting status through parentage only
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment provides that all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to its jurisdiction, are citizens. Birth on United States soil, with narrow exceptions, confers citizenship regardless of the parents' status.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Born here means citizen here: the Fourteenth Amendment rule.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a newborn nursery in a hospital with parents receiving a sealed certificate from a nurse beside a window overlooking a city skyline. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Fourteenth Amendment grants birthright citizenship.
img.title: BORN HERE, CITIZEN HERE

questions.question: An applicant for citizenship shows five years as a lawful permanent resident, continuous residence, good moral character, English and civics test passes, and takes an oath renouncing prior allegiances. Which process is she completing?
questions.correctAnswer: Naturalization, the legal process by which an immigrant becomes a United States citizen
distractors: Denaturalization, the legal process by which citizenship is granted to refugees
Registration, the legal process by which residents enroll for federal benefits
Emancipation, the legal process by which minors gain adult legal status
questions.explanation: Naturalization is the process Congress established for immigrants to become citizens, generally requiring lawful permanent residence, continuous presence, good moral character, English and civics knowledge, and an oath of allegiance. The civics test covers United States government and history.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Naturalization ends with an oath of allegiance.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of new citizens raising their right hands in a courthouse ceremony while families hold small flags from rows of folding chairs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Naturalization turns residents into citizens by law.
img.title: THE OATH OF ALLEGIANCE

questions.question: A Nashville resident serves on a jury, pays income taxes on time, registers for selective service, and also volunteers monthly at a food bank and votes in every election. Which sorting of her actions is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Jury service, taxes, and selective service registration are legal duties; volunteering and voting are civic responsibilities
distractors: Jury service and voting are legal duties; taxes and volunteering are civic responsibilities
All five actions are legal duties enforced by criminal penalties
All five actions are civic responsibilities with no legal enforcement
questions.explanation: Citizens owe legal duties enforceable by law, including obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on juries when called, and registering for selective service. Voting, volunteering, and staying informed are responsibilities of citizenship that are valued but not legally compelled.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Duties are required by law; responsibilities are expected of citizens.

questions.question: Two demographers compare states: one requires registration thirty days before voting and votes at 68 percent turnout, while the other allows same-day registration and votes at 76 percent. Which conclusion fits research on registration rules?
questions.correctAnswer: Easier registration rules, such as same-day registration, are associated with higher voter turnout
distractors: Registration deadlines have no measurable relationship to turnout in any state
Same-day registration reliably lowers turnout by confusing election officials
Turnout differences are explained entirely by the weather on election day
questions.explanation: Registration is the largest administrative hurdle to voting in the United States, and states that ease it, including through same-day registration, consistently record higher turnout. Civic duty, education, and competitiveness also raise participation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lower the paperwork barrier and turnout tends to rise.

questions.question: A state legislature draws a congressional district that snakes between three cities, gathering one party's voters into a single seat while cracking the rest across four safe seats for the other party. Which practice is being engineered?
questions.correctAnswer: Gerrymandering, the drawing of district lines to advantage one party or group
distractors: Reapportionment, the shifting of seats among states after the census
Malapportionment, the refusal to update districts for sixty years
At-large election, the practice of voting for all seats citywide
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering manipulates district boundaries through packing voters into a few districts and cracking the rest across many districts to waste their votes. Courts police racial gerrymandering, while partisan gerrymandering claims are treated as political questions in federal court after Rucho v. Common Cause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Packing and cracking: lines drawn to waste votes.

questions.question: A city bans a peaceful religious meeting while allowing identical secular meetings, and the group's lawyer argues the city's own state charter cannot save the ban because a national protection was applied to the states long ago. Which doctrine carries national rights against state and local governments?
questions.correctAnswer: Selective incorporation, applying most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment
distractors: Dual federalism, keeping the Bill of Rights aimed only at state governments
Nullification, allowing states to void the Bill of Rights within their borders
Preemption, allowing Congress to replace the Bill of Rights by statute
questions.explanation: Originally the Bill of Rights limited only the national government, as Barron v. Baltimore held. Through selective incorporation, the Supreme Court has applied most of its protections to state and local governments using the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth Amendment carries rights down to city hall.

img.tip: Selective incorporation applies rights against states.

questions.question: A state accepts federal highway money tied to a drinking age of 21, then complains that a later infrastructure grant arrives with dozens of spending conditions attached. Which modern federalism tool is the state experiencing twice?
questions.correctAnswer: Conditional federal grants, where national money comes with strings that steer state policy
distractors: Revenue sharing, where national money arrives with no policy conditions
Dual mandates, where both governments must pass identical statutes
Interstate compacts, where states jointly refuse all federal funding
questions.explanation: Modern cooperative federalism runs heavily on grants-in-aid: categorical and block grants that carry conditions states accept along with the funds. The Supreme Court upheld the drinking-age condition in South Dakota v. Dole as a valid use of the spending power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal money arrives holding federal instructions.
